items.summary:
IBM has decided to stop sponsoring H-1B visas and green cards for most positions in its U.S. consulting business, leaving affected employees with a three-week ultimatum to either transfer abroad or resign by the end of 2026.

According to The Indian Express report, those who choose to leave will receive severance equal to three months' salary, with their last working day set for December 31, 2026. IBM says it no longer wants to continue visa or green card sponsorship at these roles because its reliance on the programs has declined and skilled-worker availability plus client needs have changed; however, the company did not tie the decision directly to U.S. immigration policy.

The move could affect Indian employees disproportionately, as Indians accounted for about 71 percent of H-1B visas issued by the United States in fiscal year 2023-24. The report notes that visa rules are being tightened during President Donald Trump's second term and that in October the U.S. suspended Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme.

IBM has not clarified how many employees will ultimately be affected by the decision.
items.title: IBM Ends Visa Sponsorship for Most US Consulting Roles

items.summary:
Hyderabad's Cyber Crime police arrested two people, including the mother of the main accused, in an Instagram impersonation case that defrauded a 24-year-old software employee out of Rs 10.05 lakh (ev2). The prime accused, Jajula Gunavanth, created a fake profile using stolen photographs and posed as a wealthy doctor to win the victim's trust.

He fabricated family emergencies and induced her to transfer money and send gold ornaments through a Rapido courier service, while also fraudulently obtaining her HDFC credit card and availing a loan of Rs 2.16 lakh by misusing OTPs (ev4). His mother, Paturi Surekha alias Jajula Surekha aged 52 (ev5), allegedly received the money through digital payment accounts and was arrested on November 5, 2026 (dt6).

Police recovered approximately 20 grams of gold ornaments that were pledged for Rs 2.30 lakh at Gupta Arts and Jewellers in Banjara Hills on November 21 (ev7, ev8), along with a phone from the accused (ev3). Gunavanth had earlier been involved in a similar fraud worth Rs 20 lakh registered at Rachakonda Cyber Crime Police Station; his mother was later arrested on November 25, 2026 and produced before the IX Additional Metropolitan Magistrate Court in Kukatpally for judicial remand (ev9, dt10).

A case was filed at Cyberabad's Cyber Crime Police Station under sections 318(4), 319(2), 336(3), and 338 of the BNS along with Section 66-D of the IT Act, 2000 (ev11-ev17). The accused's cousin Borugunta Lokesh is reportedly absconding as police work to apprehend him continues.
items.title: Cyberabad Police Arrest Mother and Son in Instagram Matrimonial Fraud

items.summary:
On Thursday, November 19, Anthropic became the largest pure-play AI company to go public as the maker of the Claude line of models, and its shares jumped almost 39% above their IPO price. The race slowed a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price, giving the company a fully diluted valuation of $1.76 trillion once options, restricted stock units, and convertible notes that might one day become shares are factored in (ev2, ev3, ev4). The author noted that this figure is not bad given that the company is just five years old.

The writer then questioned what type of company it would be to raise money while issuing such stark risk warnings. Anthropic's founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in October 2023 there was a chance something goes catastrophically wrong on the scale of human civilization somewhere between 10 per cent and 25 percent (ev6, ev7), then in September 2025 stated he thinks there is a 25% chance things go really badly (ev9). Later, in January 2026, Amodei said the company is considerably closer to real danger in 2026 than it was in 2023 (dt10, dt11).

The author stressed that these estimates come from the founder and CEO himself rather than an analyst, are subjective assessments of broad AI risks including misuse and societal failures, and are neither measured Claude failure rates nor evidence of a steadily increasing numerical estimate. The writer argued that taking such warnings seriously should follow with independently verified safeguards, binding conditions on deployment, and clear accountability for harm, yet the industry appears comfortable treating these warnings as part of the investment story.

The author also pointed out that Anthropic is not alone in issuing dire forecasts. OpenAI said in February 2015 it considers superhuman machine intelligence the greatest threat to humanity's continued existence (dt13), then in June 2015 predicted AI will likely lead to the end of the world, and in January 2023 warned that the bad case is lights out for all of us (dt14, dt15). The writer closed by asking what other industry on Earth would be allowed to operate with a self-declared one-in-four chance of causing catastrophe that could wipe out humanity as a whole.
items.title: Anthropic IPOs at $97.17 With a Trillion-Dollar Valuation Amid Existential Risk Warnings

items.summary:
Actress Priyanka Chopra has drawn attention after allegedly liking an Instagram reel that described the upcoming film Ramayana as a potential box-office flop. The video, shared by copywriter and screenwriter Vivashwan Chaudhary, questioned the film's commercial prospects alongside its ambitious global collection targets and raised concerns about budget transparency, including Prime Focus' investments, rising share price, and recent Income Tax searches, while clarifying that no direct connection was being alleged between these developments. Chopra has not publicly commented on the matter.

Chaudhary shared a screenshot of her alleged like on his Instagram Story and expressed gratitude for what he called support from an influential industry figure after receiving criticism for speaking out about the film's prospects, describing her as 'my favourite.' He noted that she may have since unliked the reel to avoid controversy. The two actors previously appeared together in Anjaana Anjaani (2010) and Barfi! (2012), but Chopra has neither issued a statement nor reacted to the video.

Chaudhary's account also reported that Chopra is set to appear next in SS Rajamouli's Varanasi, alongside Mahesh Babu and Prithviraj Sukumaran. The film would mark her return to Indian cinema after 2019 and her first Telugu-language project since 2013, with a theatrical release scheduled for April 7, 2027.
items.title: Priyanka Chopra Allegedly Liked Reel Calling Ranbir Kapoor's Ramayana a Flop

items.summary:
Iran's Mehr News Agency shared an AI-generated video on Thursday through its Telegram channel depicting drone attacks on the offices of Amazon, Microsoft and SpaceX. The footage shows explosions, burning buildings and scenes of destruction accompanied by an English voiceover warning these companies that they could become targets.

The narrator states that firms involved in attacking Iran must either pay reparations and repent or face destruction on a similar scale, ending with the message 'Repentance or destruction? The choice is yours, America.' In its Persian-language post, Mehr claimed some of these companies maintain secret connections with US and Israeli military organizations and cannot avoid responsibility if they work alongside American and Israeli forces. The video also references the February bombing of an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, which killed around 175 people mostly children, noting that a preliminary military investigation found the US responsible for the missile strike.

The warning arrives as tensions between the two countries continue to rise amid ongoing military action and uncertain peace efforts. Earlier this week, President Donald Trump said further military action against Iran could occur soon after the New Year and accused Tehran of delaying peace talks. Tensions escalated after the US struck a missile launch facility on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz in response to actions by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), prompting Iran to later launch missiles and drones toward US military bases, which were intercepted by US-allied Gulf countries.

Trump criticized Iran's approach during an interview with Fox News on Sunday, describing ongoing discussions as 'all bulls***t' and comparing Iranian negotiators to 'professional tap dancers.' His comments have raised further concerns about the future of peace talks and the possibility of additional military action between the two nations.
items.title: Iranian State Media Shares AI Video Warning US Tech Firms of Possible Drone Attacks

items.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has introduced a uniform, time-bound regulatory framework allowing banks to place debit holds on transactions assessed as highly suspicious. The directions are designed to strengthen measures against cybercrime, financial fraud, and terrorist financing while protecting genuine customers from unnecessary inconvenience. They must come into effect no later than July 1, 2027.

Under the new framework, banks can initiate debit holds on accounts suspected of receiving, layering, or transferring proceeds generated through criminal offences, financial fraud, or transactions involving terrorist financing. The classification covers accounts used by individuals on their own behalf as well as money mule accounts. The RBI defines a money mule account as one used on behalf of another person to receive, layer, or transfer illicit proceeds or facilitate such transactions, irrespective of whether the account holder is aware of these activities.

The central bank clarified that not every account involving suspicious transactions automatically qualifies as a highly suspicious account requiring further intervention. Banks must deploy appropriate technological solutions and objective assessment parameters to detect potentially fraudulent transactions while minimising the risk of incorrectly flagging legitimate banking activities. Under the prescribed standard operating procedure, banks must promptly notify affected account holders through digital communication channels where their mobile numbers or email addresses are available, and by the end of the next working day when digital communication is unavailable.

Lenders must also maintain comprehensive records of amounts and accounts placed under debit hold for five years from the date of initiating the restriction. These records must include the dates on which debit holds were imposed and lifted, reasons for such actions, and details of correspondence with account holders and jurisdictional police authorities. Additionally, upon reporting a case to the jurisdictional police authority, banks must undertake enhanced due diligence of the account concerned.
items.title: RBI Introduces Framework for Debit Holds on Suspicious Transactions

items.summary:
OpenAI filed a countersuit against Apple on Friday in the Northern District of California, responding to a June lawsuit by Apple accusing it of trade secret theft. The countersuit alleges that Apple's employment practices create opportunities to accuse departing employees and their future employers of misappropriating confidential information, with OpenAI arguing that Apple can effectively target virtually any departing employee and new employer as a potential competitor.

An Apple spokesperson told CBS News on Friday that the case concerns deliberate theft and use of confidential information about unreleased products, technologies, and processes by OpenAI employees. Apple dismissed the countersuit as an attempt to divert attention from its original claims, adding that OpenAI had already been ordered to stop using Apple's confidential information.

Apple's June lawsuit accused OpenAI and two former Apple employees—Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan and technical staff member Chang Liu—of taking proprietary company information to help develop OpenAI's own hardware products. The dispute comes as OpenAI is expected to expand into hardware development, having acquired io Products Inc., an AI hardware startup founded by former Apple design chief Jony Ive, in July 2025.
items.title: OpenAI Files Countersuit Against Apple Over Trade Secret Allegations

items.summary:
An open letter signed 'Concerned Microsoft Workers' by current and former staff turns CEO Satya Nadella's own framing against his company, opening with his line that everyone is a stakeholder in AI to argue workers deserve direct input into how AI is built and used. The signatories accuse Microsoft of forcing AI tools on employees without adequate training or justification beyond speed, watering down its Community-First AI Infrastructure plan on jobs, funding for host communities, and emissions, backing away from climate goals, and accepting government contracts they say risk human rights. They set three demands: no AI without worker input and protections, no AI without community protections, and no trading environmental promises for AI gains, while also urging Microsoft to listen to its chief science officer on lobbying for rather than against regulation.

The letter gained prominence after October 26, when Microsoft offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce, in what The New York Times describes as the largest such offer in company history. The Voluntary Exit Offer covers eligible staff at level 70 and below across India, the US, UK, and Canada, excluding sales and some engineering teams; takers receive at least eight weeks of base pay scaled by tenure and level, must decide by December 9, and leave on December 31. Microsoft expects fewer than 5% to accept, chief people officer Amy Coleman called it uncharted territory not tied to AI's impact on work though she did not rule out later layoffs, and the offer followed an April early-retirement deal for around 8,600 long-serving US employees.

The letter arrives amid strong financial results that staff say have not reached them. Microsoft's September-quarter profit rose 32% to $36.6 billion, Azure sales grew 48% to $33.2 billion, capital spending climbed to $45.2 billion, and OpenAI accounted for about 11% of revenue, yet some merit raises came in below 1%. Employees told the NYT they do not expect departing colleagues replaced, which increases remaining workloads.

The unease sits within a broader pattern of job cuts: Microsoft laid off 10,000 people in 2023 and more than 15,000 in 2025, followed by about 4,800 this July. Its headcount stood at 223,000 in June, down 5,000 from a year earlier, while AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman predicted most computer-based professional work could be automated within 12 to 18 months.
items.title: Microsoft Employees Turn Nadella's AI Words Against the Company

items.summary:
Denny's reversed its decision Wednesday to reinstall an honorary plaque marking the booth where Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, then posted a lengthy tribute praising the company's shared history with the executive. The diner chain said it contacted Nvidia's communications team on November 10 to reaffirm support for Huang before learning three days later that the plaque had been removed amid reports of his extramarital affairs and alleged ties to Chinese espionage; Denny's stated its post declared 'Jensen is part of our history, and we are part of his' (The Post). The tribute drew sharp criticism online, with commenters questioning why a major diner chain weighed in on the scandal. One user called it support for an adulterer and questioned whether the company was paid to post; another suggested that if Huang meant so much to Denny's, they should have left the plaque up after initially taking it down (The Post). Others dismissed the message as tone-deaf or cringe, with one commenter joking about being a 'Disney Adult.'

Huang's personal life came under scrutiny following reports of multiple extramarital relationships involving two Nvidia employees and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence suspects has ties to Chinese espionage. Huang acknowledged his infidelity in a message to employees before resigning as CEO on November 12 (The Post). Nvidia reinstated him Monday after President Donald Trump argued that losing the longtime chief executive would harm America's ability to compete with China in artificial intelligence; Trump told The Post he might pardon Huang if necessary but expects no pardon, and urged Huang to 'tell the truth' when testifying before Congress next week.}
items.title: Denny's Restores Jensen Huang Plaque Amid Backlash Over Nvidia CEO Tribute

items.summary:
On November 27, Binance announced it had received in-principle approval from Bhutan's Gelephu Central Bank to establish regulated digital-asset operations as part of its plan to expand into five Asian markets by 2027. The company clarified that the approval is a first step rather than a full licence, and that Binance must satisfy conditions set by the central bank before any regulated activities can begin.

Binance's expansion follows an October security breach linked by US authorities to North Korea, which resulted in approximately $6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) being stolen from its platform and halted user withdrawals for two days. The company stated it had completed work on recovering its withdrawal systems that same month.

SB Seker, head of Binance's Asia-Pacific unit, told Reuters in November that the exchange was holding ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets, three of which were in mature stages, though he did not name them specifically. Binance currently holds operating licences in 15 markets, and Seker identified South and Southeast Asia as key priorities.

The Bhutan partnership is set to include an operational presence involving local hiring and investment in digital assets within Gelephu Mindfulness City. In a separate statement, Binance indicated it could cover losses from the October cyberattack without raising fresh funds.
items.title: Binance Receives Preliminary Approval for Asia Hub in Bhutan

items.summary:
Singapore and global markets rebounded after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive was announced on Nov 24, following days of tech sell-offs that wiped the year's gains from the NASDAQ. Singapore-listed counters rallied during the session, with Mi Material up 5.8% and PC Partner up 2%, though these gains eased by week's end to a 5.8% gain for Mi Material and a 2% gain for PC Partner at the Nov 27 close. Other tech stocks also finished higher, including AEM up 3.6% to $6.09 and UMS 2.5% higher at $1.64.

US markets remained volatile ahead of Thanksgiving following new tariff news, with the S&P 500 down around 2.8% over the week while NASDAQ fell nearly 5%. The Huang saga drew criticism from US lawmakers about board independence and succession planning, prompting S&P Global Ratings to place Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade on Nov 25.

Separately, Seatrium announced it would lay off around 2% of its Singapore workforce or about 220 staff as it streamlines global operations. The company has pared its yards from 15 in 2023 to the current 11 globally and plans to wind down Admiralty yard by 2028, while shares fell over 7% initially before easing to a 1.5% loss on Nov 27.

StarHub agreed to merge with M1 in a deal worth $1.1 billion, slated for completion in the first half of 2027 subject to regulatory approval by IMDA. Keppel, which owns M1's parent, said it is considering three options to monetise its stake and would receive a 23% share in the enlarged StarHub if the merger proceeds.

Singapore objected to US Section 301 findings behind proposed tariffs of up to 20% on the Republic and 13 other trading partners. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore has not confirmed whether Nvidia shipments have been stopped after new export controls, while duties could take effect in early 2027 unless a reciprocal trade agreement lowers the rate.

Investors will watch for final tariff decisions, US manufacturing and consumer data over the week, and Huang's scheduled Senate Banking Committee testimony on Dec 3 regarding US export controls and AI chip security.
items.title: Tech rebounds; Seatrium retrenches over 200 staff; StarHub, M1 to merge: Markets this week

A report from The Economic Times states that mutual fund Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) contributions reached approximately Rs 3.5 lakh crore in fiscal year 2026, roughly 3.5 times the level six years earlier. New SIP registrations rose from about 2.7 crore in FY2022 to 7.2 crore in FY2026, and cumulative net additions over this period stood at approximately 6.7 crore, equivalent to nearly 64% of outstanding SIP accounts.

Equity-oriented schemes accounted for 84% of SIP contributions, representing an estimated 37% of gross resource mobilisation by equity schemes in FY2026. Industry assets under management expanded about 2.3 times over the five-year period, rising from around Rs 32 lakh crore in March 2021 to Rs 74 lakh crore in March 2026, with growth-oriented equity scheme AUM growing by 3.3 times to Rs 32 lakh crore and its share of overall industry AUM climbing to 43% from 30%. The report also notes that the passive investment product share nearly doubled to 19% in March 2026 from 10%, debt-oriented and hybrid schemes grew at a compound annual growth rate of around 8% during this period, B30 location contributions rose to 18% of overall AUM from nearly 15%, the retail direct-plan share increased to 32% from 12%, and high-net-worth individual direct investing rose to 30% from 21%. The article includes a disclaimer that expert recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions are their own and do not represent those of The Economic Times.

India and the United States continue negotiating a trade deal built on an interim agreement announced on February 7, 2026, while India prepares for its free trade agreement with the European Union. The commerce ministry said in a Saturday statement that the India-EU FTA is expected to come into effect in early 2027, following formal signing by mid-December during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Brussels visit and at least three-to-four months of post-signing operationalization. Commerce minister Piyush Goyal stated on Friday that the deal would take effect by March or April next year.

Under the India-EU agreement, duties will end upon entry into force for 70.4% of the EU's tariff lines, covering 90.7% of India's export value, with a further 20.3% of tariff lines being phased out over time. People close to development said, requesting anonymity, that India would sign the proposed interim bilateral trade agreement only after all tariff uncertainties are resolved, including responses to the United States Trade Representative's Section 301 investigation into excess capacity and product-specific Section 232 actions.

The USTR office proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods following an investigation into structural excess capacity in manufacturing. The rate would fall to 17% if India reaches an agreement, a point below the 18% agreed in February's interim framework and below rates proposed for export rivals such as Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand at 18%, plus Vietnam at 20%. Exporters have questioned how much that edge is worth.

The statement also described a sixth round of negotiations with Canada held from November 11-20, aimed at securing an agreement benefiting farmers, industries, businesses and MSMEs. Negotiations are underway with Chile, Peru, Israel, the Eurasian Economic Union, Mexico and other partners. Commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal addressed exporters during outreach initiatives in Jaipur and Dehradun on Friday.

The ministry cited Piyush Goyal's note that India's preferential access to global markets expanded from around USD 10 trillion in GDP a few years ago by an additional USD 60 trillion over four-and-a-half years, reaching approximately USD 70 trillion. The statement projected this could expand to around $85 trillion, representing nearly 76% of global GDP, over the next year and a half.
items.title: India Continues US Trade Talks While Targeting Early 2027 EU FTA Rollout

items.summary: On 25 November 2026, the US Office of Trade Representative released its Section 301 report on India under the US Trade Act of 1974. The document frames Indian manufacturing as suffering from structural excess capacity that justifies tariffs, yet it also acknowledges what Washington calls success in building production beyond market levels. It identifies Make in India, Production Linked Incentive schemes, and Atmanirbhar Bharat as the chief drivers behind this expansion.
items.title: Trump tariffs

The Telangana High Court has expressed serious reservations about the State Bank of India advancing a loan of nearly Rs 500 crore to M/s Sem India Fab Pvt Ltd for establishing a semiconductor manufacturing facility at Fab City near Hyderabad, even though the project had made no tangible progress. Justice Nagesh Bheempaka questioned why the bank sanctioned such a large loan when the company had failed to make substantial investments against a proposed total of around Rs 20,000 crore, observing that collateral or mortgage alone could not justify advancing an enormous sum without evidence of adequate assessment of repayment capacity.

The court suo motu impleaded the Central Bureau of Investigation in Hyderabad as a respondent and directed the Registry to provide it with case records. The dispute concerns 100 acres allotted under a February 16, 2006 memorandum of understanding for an ATMP semiconductor unit planned at roughly $2.25 billion; the government resumed 78 acres on February 9, 2010, while SBI claimed it advanced loans around Rs 500 crore based on NOCs and a mortgage created in August 2011.

The judge noted that the loan was sanctioned more than a year after land resumption began, that government NOCs did not transfer title since ownership remained with TGIIC, and that even by 2022 only an unfinished shed stood on the remaining 22 acres. The court found no material showing the company had invested as much as 50 or 75 per cent of its proposed cost before seeking the loan.

Emphasising established banking principles, the High Court observed that a borrower's sources of repayment should be primary rather than collateral alone, and noted neither SBI nor the company demonstrated adequate due diligence. The matter was posted to December 4, 2026.
items.title: Telangana HC questions SBI's Rs 500-cr bet on stalled semiconductor project

Union parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju on Saturday urged the Congress party to set aside political differences and support the government's Delimitation Bill, arguing that concerns raised by various states and communities had already been addressed. He said Prime Minister Narendra Modi made a proposal designed to take into account every state while ensuring 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies (ev1). Rijiju appealed to Congress members as well as those opposing the bill at their behest to join hands in Parliament, framing the measure as an effort toward women's empowerment. He said the proposed legislation would not only provide that 33% reservation but also increase the number of elected representatives in Parliament and state assemblies (ev2).

Rijiju accused Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge of opposing a democratic process, saying 'The Congress party has never believed in democracy' and questioning why they opposed a bill aimed at empowering women. He suggested that Rahul Gandhi may have influenced Kharge's position but added he could not say so with certainty (ev5). The Centre is set to introduce the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, in the Lok Sabha on Monday to implement one-third reservation for women across Parliament and state and Union territory legislative assemblies through a fresh delimitation exercise.

Rijiju noted that this proposed legislation differs from the earlier Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, which was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April, mainly in its approach to delimitation, the allocation of seats among states, and the census data used for redrawing constituencies.
items.title: Rijiju Urges Congress to Back Delimitation Bill

items.summary:
A compromise signed on October 12, 1968 was intended to settle a land dispute over the Katra Keshav Dev complex in Mathura, where the Lord Krishna Janmabhoomi temple and Shahi Eidgah mosque stand. The agreement laid down boundaries between the two structures, specified which portions each side would receive, and sought to prevent future disputes over access and construction.

Nearly 58 years later, Hindu litigants argue that the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sangh lacked authority to compromise property belonging to the deity. The Muslim side has relied on the agreement and civil court decrees from 1973 and 1974 to contend that the dispute was already settled.

On November 20, 2026, Justice Avnish Saxena of the Allahabad high court dismissed an application seeking a declaration that the October 12, 1968 agreement was null and void. The dismissal also sought cancellation of decrees passed in 1973 and 1974 and delivery of vacant possession to the deity.

The court held that this relief could not be decided through an interim application because it formed part of connected suits requiring a trial, so the order was made without affecting the merits of those cases. The next hearing is scheduled for December 10.

In its August 1, 2024 judgment, the Allahabad high court recorded the historical narrative advanced by Hindu plaintiffs and allowed their suits to proceed rather than dismissing them at threshold under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The court observed that questions about the legality and validity of the agreement were factual issues requiring evidence during trial.

The dispute concerns a 13.37-acre property, which Hindu plaintiffs claim was dedicated through a trust deed dated March 9, 1951 to the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi Trust. The plaintiffs argue that this trust and the Seva Sangh were separate legal entities, with the latter neither owning the property nor having authority over it.

Advocate Kanu Agarwal told TOI that 'the deity or the trust were never the parties to Civil Suit No. 43 of 1967 or to the compromise deed dated 12.10.1968.' He described the Seva Sangh as a distinct legal entity from the Janmabhoomi Trust and stated that it 'prima facie was not the owner of the suit property.'

The plaintiffs further contend that neither the deity nor the trust was a party to Civil Suit No. 43 of 1967 or the subsequent settlement, arguing that the Seva Sangh conceded land it had no right to surrender.

Defendants have contested this position by noting that the compromise was entered into by recognised representatives with Waqf Board permission obtained through a letter dated September 9, 1968. The Muslim side has relied on subsequent civil court decrees and argued that a challenge cannot be brought through fresh proceedings.

The central legal question remains whether the Seva Sangh had authority to enter into the compromise, whether it could bind the deity and trust, and what effect should attach to the 1973 and 1974 decrees. The Allahabad high court has not delivered a final verdict on these matters.

The current litigation gained momentum in 2020 when advocate Ranjana Agnihotri and six others filed a suit seeking ownership of the property, removal of the Shahi Eidgah structure, and restoration of the temple. This raised broader debate around the Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991.

Advocate Kanu Agarwal said 'the compromise deed of 1968 has no bearing or connection with [the] Places of Worship Act,' adding that the site's religious character and title would require detailed trial. In May 2022, AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi questioned the revival of the dispute by tweeting that 'Sri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sangh and the Shahi Idgah Trust had resolved their issues by an agreement in 1968,' asking why it was being revived now.

The Hindu side maintained that the agreement was not binding on the deity and needed examination by a court. A survey of the disputed premises remains linked to Supreme Court proceedings, with Justice Avnish Saxena noting he could not pass a fresh order until the Supreme Court finally adjudicated the pending petition.
items.title: Allahabad High Court Defers on Validity of 1968 Mathura Compromise

The China Wildlife Conservation Association (CWCA) announced that giant panda Ran Ran departed Saturday for Belgium to join a bilateral conservation and research program with the Belgian wildlife park Pairi Daiza. The adult female, born May 31, 2017, comes from the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda and will participate under a supplementary agreement signed in September 2026 until its scheduled conclusion in February 2029.

The CWCA said both sides made extensive preparations to ensure Ran Ran's safe arrival. Before departure, she underwent quarantine and a medical examination in China and was found healthy, while Chinese experts inspected the panda facilities at Pairi Daiza and provided technical guidance. Food, water, and medical supplies including bamboo shoots and carrots were prepared for her journey, accompanied by a Chinese veterinarian and a Belgian keeper.

Pairi Daiza also upgraded its panda facilities and secured a stable long-term supply of edible bamboo ahead of Ran Ran's arrival. The park assembled an experienced animal care team and established comprehensive management procedures and technical standards in preparation for the panda.

In the 2026 Victorian election, Ben Carroll conceded defeat to Jess Wilson as Coalition won majority government and ended 12 years of Labor rule. At 36, Wilson will become Victoria's youngest leader since federation and its first popularly elected woman premier; Carroll also lost his seat of Niddrie after Labor held it for its entire 50-year history, marking the first time a Victorian premier has lost their own seat at a state election.

Carroll addressed party members shortly after 8.30pm, taking full responsibility and describing democracy as 'brutal,' while deputy leader Gabrielle Williams urged the party to learn from its mistakes and revisit lessons from 2022. The Greens secured seven seats so far—holding Brunswick, Richmond, and Melbourne, and winning Pascoe Vale, Preston off Labor and Prahran off the Liberals—with Sarah Mansfield calling early results a vindication of their progressive agenda.

Guardian Australia has called several Labor seats for the Liberals, including Frankston, Mordialloc in the south-east, Hastings on the Mornington Peninsula, Box Hill and Ringwood in the eastern suburbs, plus South Barwon—the party's first win off Labor there since the 1990s—and Point Cook, Sydenham, Werribee, and Melton. If current trends continue, the Greens may ultimately hold more lower house seats than state Labor, potentially becoming official opposition; meanwhile federal Labor sources distanced themselves from the result.
items.title: Ben Carroll Concedes to Jess Wilson, Ending Labor's Victorian Government

Claire Jackson, a journalist covering classical music, art, and animals, describes her quirk of writing cheques by hand, noting that a younger colleague recently watched with bemusement as she filled one out for South East Water. The colleague had never seen a chequebook before and believed the process would be better executed online, while a friend also suggested using a bank transfer instead.

Jackson argues that paying by cheque is genuinely ideal because it offers enjoyment through holding a pen or pencil and selecting appropriate ink colors, with graphite being unacceptable. She adds that cheques prevent hasty financial transactions after she once found herself in debt, contrasting this with the risk of accidentally tapping contactless payments without checking amounts.

She highlights inherent trust required to accept cheques as adding to their appeal, citing The Harrow Inn pub in Steep, Hampshire, which refuses credit or debit cards but welcomed her lunch on a day when she had neither cash nor card. She acknowledges unexpected benefits of digital banking through an anecdote about a young boy who used his Monzo account to buy snacks aboard a Thames Clipper while his mother was distracted.

Despite these advantages, Jackson reveals that HMRC recently informed her she overpaid tax and outlined refund options, after which she selected the cheque method for receiving her money.
items.title: Journalist Defends Cheques as the Ideal Way to Pay

Monia Indge, a 58-year-old woman with terminal cancer, was told she was banned for life from Sainsbury's after staff used facial recognition technology to falsely identify her as someone flagged in the FaceWatch system. The incident occurred on 7 November at the Walters Yard branch in Bromley while she shopped with her husband; a member of staff directed her to scan a QR code that led to the FaceWatch website, and security guards escorted her from the store without explaining why.

Indge said being surrounded by security guards was frightening and left her feeling traumatised and violated. Ten days later Sainsbury's apologised, attributing the incident to human error and offering a £150 voucher (ev3). FaceWatch confirmed that in both cases its system correctly flagged individuals it was looking for, but described the human check before acting on an alert as an important safeguard.

Indge is one of several people misidentified by FaceWatch; Oleh Sinkevych, 44, was asked to leave a Sainsbury's branch in Canada Water on 24 October and received an apology email identical to Indge's (ev4). Jack Coulson of Big Brother Watch said live facial recognition had turned shop workers into 'untrained police officers' and urged the ICO to act. The Information Commissioner's Office noted that such technology must comply with data protection law, while a Sainsbury's spokesperson cited eight in ten people added to the system not returning to reoffend.
items.title: Sainsbury's Woman Traumatized by Facial Recognition Shoplifting Ban

items.summary:
In the Alaka'i plateau of remote Kaua'i, Hawaiian honeycreepers are collapsing as mosquitoes carrying avian malaria push into higher forest. The 'akikiki was declared lost last year after its wild population vanished, and the 'akekeke is down to a handful in the wild. Olive-green 'amakihi dropped from around 9,000 birds in 2023 to under 500 this year, while the 'anianiau fell from more than 3,000 individuals in 2023 to only a few hundred. In June researchers told local lawmakers that every endemic honeycreeper species on Kaua'i could be lost as soon as Christmas.

Lisa Crampton of the Kaua'i Forest Bird Recovery Project said mosquito numbers exploded after an unprecedented swarm reached higher elevations, rising from about one or three mosquitoes per trap per night to 300 per trap per night within two months. Justin Hite of the Hawai'i Division of Forestry and Wildlife noted that this mosquito storm was more devastating than a hurricane like Hurricane Lowell, which struck Kaua'i on September 7th. Professor Jeff Foster attributed rising temperatures from global climate change as the main driver pushing mosquitoes higher; he also said drier conditions favor mosquitoes in Hawaii contrary to usual assumptions, and that plateau-shaped mountains left few birds in a transition zone so the decline went unnoticed until it appeared sudden.

A 2026 paper published in the Journal of Ecology and Evolution by John Neddermeyer's team found mosquitoes arrived on Hawaiian Islands at the beginning of the 19th century via European whaling ships, then only reached higher elevations recently as warming drew them upward. Foster noted that between 18 percent and 35 percent of birds globally carry avian malaria but rarely suffer mass mortality events; honeycreepers are especially vulnerable because they evolved without mosquitoes over millions of years and lack immunity.

Conservationists have shifted from mosquito eradication to relocating birds, currently holding three species in captivity: 19 'anianiau, 30 'akikiki, and three 'akekeke. Loren Sackett of the University of Louisiana led discovery of a gene conferring avian malaria resistance in O'ahu and Hawai'i 'amakihi, though CRISPR gene-editing is considered too new for wild birds by both Foster and Sackett. Hybridization between Kaua'i and O'ahu 'amakihi remains possible but faces legal and ethical challenges under the Endangered Species Act's case-by-case approach.

Justin Hite said his team lacks time or resources to pursue genetic options, noting that only a handful of related captive females remain for Kaua'i 'amakihi. Crampton hopes translocating abundant 'anianiau to higher forests on Hawai'i island will buy time; she acknowledged the move is temporary and carries risks since the birds have never existed there. Hite said more than 3,000 'anianiau died in the last three years, leaving only a handful. Both Hite and Crampton agreed that rising temperatures mean mosquitoes will eventually reach high-elevation forests across all Hawaiian islands.
items.title: Mosquitoes Spread Avian Malaria Up Kaua'i Forests, Threatening Endemic Honeycreepers

items.summary:
An interview between Inside Climate News host Steve Curwood and author David Helvarg, drawn from his book 'Forest of the Sea: The Remarkable Life and Imperiled Future of Kelp,' centers on kelp forests as among Earth's most productive ecosystems. Helvarg says these forests cover nearly 1 million square miles along colder coastlines (ev1) and generate about 20 percent of the planet's oxygen, a figure he attributes to algae that photosynthesize alongside estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves and seagrasses (ev3). He describes them as the 'Amazon of the ocean,' noting they span more territory than the Amazon rainforest. Helvarg also highlights kelp seaweed as an agricultural product worth about $500 billion a year, with roughly 140 million tons produced annually versus 90 million tons wild-caught (ev4, ev5), including 30 million tons of seaweeds and kelps specifically (ev6, ev7). He points out that most people are unaware kelp is about 40 percent alginate used in processed foods, toothpaste and cosmetics (ev8).

Helvarg explains the decline driving his concern. Twenty years ago he says mechanical harvesting, overfishing and pollution were the main threats to coral and kelp; today he identifies ocean warming as the overwhelming problem, with 80 percent of the ocean experiencing marine heat waves at some point last year (ev12). He cites a Prince William Sound event where temperatures reached about 76 degrees and killed all kelp and dependent species (ev15), plus an ocean 'blob' between 2013 and 2017 that removed roughly 95 percent of bull kelp in Northern California (dt16, dt17, ev18). He details a cascade there: the loss supercharged sea star wasting disease, wiping out about 99 percent of sunflower sea stars, which let purple urchins devour kelp forests across some 350 miles and form 'urchin barrens' (ev22), requiring removal of roughly 6 million urchins over a decade to restore an area he visited measuring around 80 acres (dt17, ev24).

Helvarg notes recovery is possible when conditions are right. He points to South Korea's fisheries agency investing about $29 million annually in restoration and restoring some 50,000 acres with plans for roughly 130,000 by 2030 (ev19). He also emphasizes intact predator systems like sea otters that keep kelp-destroying urchins in check. A Nature report he references suggests expanding kelp forests could cost about $14 billion; Congress is considering a 'Help Our Kelp' bill funding roughly $5 million annually for restoration and research (ev20). Helvarg concludes that without ending fossil fuel use by the end of the century, real kelp forests will not survive.
items.title: Author Argues Kelp Forests Are Vital Ocean Carbon Sinks Threatened by Marine Heat Waves

items.summary:
UK online benefits and pensions services remained offline on Saturday morning following a cyber incident that forced the government to take them down late Thursday. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has not confirmed what triggered the shutdown but has not ruled out hacking, while Downing Street declined to say whether DWP had been targeted.

Experts offered differing assessments of the cause: David Knott, former chief technology officer, said his strong suspicion was that hackers were involved; John Curry of Bath Spa University argued the department almost certainly detected and shut down activity to prevent data theft. The government assured recipients that payments would continue despite some claimants reporting delays it does not believe are linked to the incident.

The shutdown affected Pip applications and the Tell Us Once death registration system, with DWP making around 2.5 million payments daily. Officials said no personal information had been lost or stolen and that they were working with GCHQ's National Cyber Security Centre on the investigation. The PCS union criticized IT investment levels and noted a voluntary redundancy scheme in the technology division opened days before the incident.

The government pointed to a £210m cyber action plan as evidence of its security spending, while Shadow AI minister Ben Spencer called the incident deeply concerning over whether higher standards could be demanded without protecting own systems. The event added to broader concerns about state system vulnerability and the role of advancing AI technology in aiding hackers.
items.title: Pensions and benefits services still down after 'cyber incident'

Paul de Villiers is set to start at number eight in the back row for South Africa against France in the Nations Championship final at Twickenham on Sunday, according to a revised team announced by the Springboks. The reshuffle follows an injury to Pieter-Steph du Toit and moves Cameron Hanekom into Du Toit's number seven jersey.

De Villiers was initially named on the bench when the squad was first announced but comes into the starting XV at the back of the scrum, with captain Siya Kolisi joining him in the loose-forward trio. Franco Mostert is among those moved to the replacements, which also include Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche, Wilco Louw, Eben Etzebeth, Emmanuel Tshituka, Morne van den Berg and Canan Moodie.

The Springboks have lost their last two tests to France and Ireland but still finished top of the Southern Hemisphere pool. They meet France again in the decider after finishing atop that group.
items.title: De Villiers Named at Number Eight for Springboks

Vox has centered its campaign on immigration ahead of Sunday's snap election in Spain, according to a report by Vox. The party made the issue central after tens of thousands of migrants streamed into Ceuta from Morocco in July, an event that dominated politics and shaped the electoral focus.

Immigration emerged as the key theme for the upcoming vote, with the influx into the north African city serving as the backdrop against which the campaign has developed.
items.title: Immigration Dominates Vox Campaign Ahead of Spanish Snap Election

items.summary:
Restaurant owners across the UK are reverting to telephone bookings after a wave of artificial intelligence bots began swarming online reservation systems, with some venues reporting that even phone calls cannot fully deter them. Meta's newly launched Muse assistant in the UK can make restaurant reservations and shop on users' behalf once granted access to their email, and it has reportedly caused chaos for restaurants following millions of downloads in the US.

Dave Strauss, co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was recently named UK restaurant of the year, said he answered an unnerving call from a bot that sounded realistic but admitted 'Yes this is an AI booking process,' after which he told it to never call him again. Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge who books for celebrities via WhatsApp or phone, described the situation as terrifying and warned of potential chaos, noting she values personal relationships with venues because apps reveal nothing about whether clients will actually show up.

The problem has been especially pronounced in New York City, where hard-to-secure tables are a status symbol; 4 Charles Prime Rib, known for its wagyu cheeseburger topped with a fried egg, was targeted by AI agents and forced Resy to ban multiple accounts using bots. Strauss said his business believes the push toward automation 'doesn't work' and that he would gladly get rid of online booking if possible.

Jeremy King, who owns Simpson's in the Strand among other venues, said the depersonalisation brought by AI is pushing him back toward a more analogue approach while remaining open to new technology. Meta has deals with British businesses including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury's and easyJet that let Muse navigate their websites or apps, accessing sites directly if no connector app exists.

The Information Commissioner's Office said on Tuesday that Meta had committed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme after talks about complying with UK laws before the launch, while the Competition and Markets Authority reported changes were made to make the app's terms fairer. Meta has been contacted for comment.
items.title: UK Restaurant Owners Turn Back to Phones as AI Booking Bots Cause Chaos

items.summary:
Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) is preparing to release tickets for the special Vaikunta Dwara Darshan at the Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple in Tirumala, with the darshan facility set to run for 10 days from December 20 to 29. According to a Times of India report, TTD officials have finalized an online booking schedule across different categories of tickets and tokens so devotees can plan their pilgrimage.

The announced schedule lists Srivani Darshan tickets releasing first on November 28 at 10 am (ev1), followed by ₹300 Special Entry Darshan tickets on November 30. Online registration for Slotted Sarva Darshan tokens through the electronic dip system opens December 1 and closes December 5, with e-Dip allocation of those tokens scheduled for December 7.

In view of expected heavy crowds during the festival, TTD has decided to cancel VIP Break Darshan except for protocol dignitaries, along with ₹300 Special Entry Darshan tickets on December 20 and 21 (ev2). During these two days devotees can access darshan only through online e-Dip Slotted Sarva Darshan tokens. The decision aims to allow a larger number of ordinary devotees to participate in the special darshan during the peak festival period.

Separately, TTD sources say that after a Chennai-based couple donated gold ornaments to Lord Venkateswara, arrangements were made on Friday to adorn the deity with the newly donated jewellery. Donors Vardhaman Jain and Radhika Jain presented 46 different gold ornaments (ev3) weighing a total of 121 kg and valued at approximately ₹208 crore (ev5), which TTD sources describe as the largest offering ever made by an individual devotee to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala.
items.title: TTD to Release Vaikunta Dwara Darshan Tickets From November 28; Cancels VIP Break and Special Entry on Festival Days

items.summary:
Professional wrestler Bronson Reed, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, has died at age 38 from medical complications on Friday, WWE announced. The company did not provide further details about the cause of death and offered condolences to his family, including pregnant wife Paige and their daughter, describing him as a devoted family man and beloved colleague before contacting them for comment.

Haley was honored during a WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday. The show opened with a 10-bell salute (ev1), and Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband reading 'Bronson' while addressing the crowd about how much Haley loved performing and his family.

WWE greats posted tributes online, including retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair (ev2) and Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page. Eddie Guerrero is noted as another wrestler who died at age 38 in 2005 from heart failure (dt3). Haley signed with WWE in 2019 after competing on the independent scene, was released in 2021 before returning a year later and continuing until his death, and won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.

According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh earlier in November. He did not have a match at that event but was thrown off stage through tables during a brawl. Reed is described as the second wrestler to die in recent months after Benjamin Satterley passed away aged 40 in September.
items.title: WWE wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38

items.summary:
Bennett Butchers in Spalding, Lincolnshire, is preparing to close after operating for 127 years. The shop was opened by Henry Bennett in 1899 and is now owned by Andrew Parsons, his great-grandson.

Parsons said the business remained popular and profitable but had become 'unviable' due to rising costs, including a National Insurance hike from the government last year and higher energy use. He noted that while the shop was still profitable, it was less so than before, and required significant investment to continue operating.

A HM Treasury spokesperson said the government offered business rates support and measures to cut firm costs, doubling the Employment Allowance for reducing National Insurance liability to £10,500 and cutting electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 eligible businesses. Parsons thanked residents for their outpouring of support since announcing the closure on 18 October, noting the shop had sold more meat in the following six weeks than it would over two Christmases.

He also praised staff who faced redundancy but secured new jobs and described an anonymous plaque celebrating the business's customer service as 'fantastic' and 'amazing.' Parsons said he planned to relax after closing since it was his first Christmas without working for 44 years, though he hoped to remain in the meat industry rather than retire.
items.title: Butcher Blames Rising Costs for Closure After 127 Years

items.summary:
Australia's conservatives hope for victory in trendsetting state

Victoria's state election, held on Saturday near Melbourne, is seen as a potential blow to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's centre-left Labor party, which has governed the region for 12 years. Opinion polls projected that Liberal Party leader Jess Wilson could widely oust incumbent Premier Ben Carroll; if she succeeds, she would become the first Liberal woman to serve as premier of what Australia's business newspaper, the Australian Financial Review, calls 'Australia's toughest job.'

Wilson is a 36-year-old first-term lawmaker whose main pledge is reducing Victoria's debt through measures totalling Aus$20 billion (€12.2 billion), including a controversial plan to privatise the sewerage system. She told Channel 7 that she believes the election will be closer than polls suggest, and argued that a Labor defeat would add pressure on the Prime Minister amid record-low approval ratings tied to rising living costs.

The country's central bank reportedly raised interest rates again to an 18-year high, citing prolonged conflict in the Middle East and inflationary pressures. Far-right anti-immigration One Nation party leader Pauline Hanson said her party could win seats for the first time and play a kingmaker role; she told media that Labor is 'out of the state' and claimed the Liberals could not have won without One Nation's help.
items.title: Victoria state election expected to challenge Labor

items.summary: Lu You, a 12th-century Chinese poet, was among the first to explore the inner lives of cats. The item is presented as part of Eco India's Episode 340, which focuses on how citizens across cities are championing clean and accessible mobility.
items.title: Eco India Episode 340 Explores Clean and Accessible Urban Mobility

items.summary:
Anusua Mukherjee, deputy editor of Frontline, reflects on the sesquicentenary of Rassundari Devi's Amar Jiban (My Life), which she notes is being reissued by Writers Workshop Kolkata in a new edition of Enakshi Chatterjee's 1999 translation. The memoir was published around 1876 and marks one of the earliest examples of women's writing in Bengali, written at age 88 by a woman born near 1809 who married at 12 and had 12 children, seven of whom survived.

Mukherjee observes that although Amar Jiban does not read as radical on its surface—its flat voice presents social conventions as endured realities rather than questioned ones—the text is more complex. She points to Rassundari's use of divine attribution for her desire to learn reading and specifically references the Chaitanya Bhagavata, noting that Jyotirindranath Tagore's introduction suggests this strategy successfully deflected criticism.

She connects the memoir to contemporary translation work through Bloomsbury's 5 Stories series, which includes anthologies of long short stories translated from Kannada, Konkani, Marathi, Sinhala, Malayalam, and Urdu. Mukherjee quotes reviewer Rohini Mokashi-Punekar as calling these stories 'surprisingly impactful and deeply affecting,' while noting that the conditions described in Amar Jiban persist 150 years later.

The piece closes with a personal anecdote about her grandmother's illiterate mother versus her literate, English-educated daughter. Mukherjee uses this contrast to argue that if patriarchy is timeless, so too is defiance.
items.title: Frontline marks 150 years since Rassundari Devi's Bengali autobiography

items.summary: Mini Krishnan serves as series editor for two anthologies collecting long short stories in Kannada and Konkani, offering introductions that frame translation as a means of cultural travel away from sterile homogenisation. The reviewer notes that all 10 stories employ realism while portraying non-elite characters whose lives are obscured by social position or gender (ev1). Susheela Punitha and Vidya Pai strengthen the realistic mode in their translations, often rendering spoken sociolects without italics to immerse readers in the original cultural worlds. The Kannada anthology contains five stories bookended by two women authors: Vaidehi's 'Worlds within Worlds' examines Brahminical patriarchy through a trapped bride and Dalit woman whose agency comes only through labour, while Banu Mushtaq's 'Not a Woman', rooted in the Bandaya movement, explores how class undermines religious precept (ev2). Other Kannada selections include Bolwar Kunhi's 'Worship,' Amaresh Nugadoni's tea-stall story set against Kargil and cricket that probes nationalism and religious polarisation, Mogalli Ganesh's Dalit-focused 'The Spinning Top,' plus works by Vaidehi and Banu Mushtaq. The anthology is published by Bloomsbury India at 200 pages for Rs.499 (ev3). Vidya Pai situates the Konkani stories within the language's recent literary emergence following its Sahitya Akademi recognition in 1975 and Eighth Schedule inclusion in 1992, featuring five writers from Goa including Jnanpith awardee Damodar Mauzo. The reviewed works include Mauzo's 'Cry Now' on Goan Catholic traditions, Pundalik Naik's 'Jait' about impoverished agricultural labourers, Jayanti Naik's and Mahabaleshwar Sail's laments for vanishing rural life, and Prakash S. Parienkar's experimental environmental story (dt4). The reviewer concludes that both anthologies chart little-known cultural terrains of India in original ways and recommends them highly; the author is Rohini Mokashi-Punekar, whose 2023 book on Mahatma Phule appears separately (dt5, dt6).
items.title: Anthologies of Kannada and Konkani Short Stories

items.summary:
The Economic Times explains systematic withdrawal plans (SWPs) as a method for retirees to generate regular income from a fixed savings corpus after they no longer have salary or other steady earnings. Under an SWP, an investor invests a lump sum in a mutual fund scheme and then withdraws a fixed amount at regular intervals.

Many mutual fund analysts believe that SWPs are more beneficial than dividends for obtaining regular money because equity-mutual-fund dividends depend on market movements and the profit earned by the fund house rather than being guaranteed. The publication notes that an SWP calculator shows the balance remaining after all withdrawals, requiring inputs such as total investment amount, monthly withdrawal needed, expected annual rate of return, and total investment horizon.

The article provides a step-by-step calculation using the PMT formula to determine the closing value or balance left after withdrawing amounts at regular intervals. The example instructs readers to enter their lumpsum investment amount, the desired monthly withdrawal, an assumed 12% rate of return (ev3), and a 10-year withdrawal horizon before entering opening balance, withdrawal amount, returns, and closing balance.

The piece carries a disclaimer that recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by experts are their own and do not represent the views of The Economic Times. Readers can submit mutual fund queries to ET Mutual Funds via Facebook/Twitter or email at ETMFqueries@timesinternet.in along with age, risk profile, and Twitter handle.
items.title: Systematic Withdrawal Plans Offer Regular Income From Mutual Funds

items.summary:
Search crews rescued a group of hikers who became trapped by rising floodwaters at Lerderderg Gorge in central Victoria. According to Victoria Police, the 11 hikers were caught in the gorge around 10:30am when swelling waters blocked their escape route after they had set out amid significant rain across the state.

The rescue was carried out with a Victoria Police helicopter guiding the group to safety along a high ridge line. Lerderderg Gorge is part of the Wombat-Lerderderg National Park, which spans 44,000 hectares and draws visitors as a popular attraction.

Victoria Police reported that no one was injured in the incident. The State Emergency Service Bacchus Marsh Unit has urged hikers to avoid both the Werribee and Lerderderg Gorge until floodwaters recede.
items.title: Victoria Police Rescue Hikers Trapped in Lerderderg Gorge Floodwaters

items.summary:
Lander Van Tricht, a postdoctoral researcher at ETH Zürich and Vrije Universiteit in Brussels, developed the Global Glacier Extinction Explorer to make glacier research accessible beyond academia and help communities prepare for glacier loss. The interactive platform lets users zoom into individual glaciers on a map colored by extinction timing—orange and red indicating earlier disappearance—and click them to see projected extinction years across four warming scenarios of 1.5°C, 2°C, 2.7°C, and 4°C that mirror IPCC levels used in the Paris Agreement framework.

The tool is based on Van Tricht's lead-authored study published in Nature Climate Change in 2026, which found that even under a best-case warming limit of 1.5°C above pre-industrial baseline, half of Earth's glaciers will be lost and those losses are already locked in. In mountain ranges with small glaciers such as the Alps and Caucasus, nearly all glaciers disappear by around 4.9°F (2.7°C) because they are highly sensitive to warming.

Van Tricht said he was surprised by how fast glacier loss is occurring when measured at the individual-glacier level rather than just volume or area for sea-level rise purposes. He noted that in the Pyrenees, about 15 glaciers remain today and all could disappear within roughly 10-15 years, while even Aletsch Glacier—the largest in the Alps—could vanish before century's end under a 4°C (7.2°F) world despite holding around 15 cubic kilometers of ice now.

Van Tricht said limiting global warming is the only way to save glaciers: at 1.5°C, about 400 glaciers remain in the Alps versus just 20 at 4°C, so lower warming preserves more glacier area. He cited positive trends toward green energy as a source of hope and mentioned local measures like geotextiles used in ski resorts, though he noted these are expensive and polluting.

Van Tricht shared an example of public engagement when a woman wrote him that she visited a glacier at age 10 only to learn it would disappear by 2063 according to the tool. The study was co-authored with colleagues including Farinotti, D., published in Nature Climate Change volume 16 on pages 143-147.
items.title: Glacier extinction explorer shows half of Earth's glaciers lost even at 1.5°C

items.summary:
Speaking at CNBC Awaaz's Market Mahakumbh event, Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the regulator is working on a proposal to create a separate trading platform for pre-IPO shares and that work was already underway. He added that a consultation paper would be released soon and framed the idea as one of several measures being examined amid significant expansion in India's IPO market over the past three to four years.

Pandey clarified that the proposed exchange would cover only companies preparing to launch an IPO, not the entire unlisted market, which he said comprises lakhs of companies. He emphasized that investor protection and safeguards would be central to designing the mechanism, including additional disclosure requirements, before a framework is finalized.

The announcement followed Sebi's November 23 advisory cautioning investors against grey market premium figures, which it described as unofficial, unverified and unregulated premiums circulated through websites, digital platforms and newspapers. The regulator also stated that these figures have no regulatory backing despite being presented as indicators of an IPO's expected listing price or potential returns.

Separately, Pandey said Sebi aims to reduce the time for foreign portfolio investors to complete onboarding from several months to as little as five business days, part of a broader review covering IPOs, corporate bonds and market technology. He also noted that Sebi proposed removing the Additional Disclosure Framework for FPIs to align India's rules with global standards.

At an ASSOCHAM conference in New Delhi, Pandey outlined four priorities: simplifying regulations, deepening markets to support economic growth, facilitating access for global investors, and expanding technology use while maintaining safeguards. He cited that India's equity market valuation crossed Rs 500 trillion, equivalent to more than 130% of GDP, and that companies raised around Rs 9 trillion through equity and debt markets in the first seven months of the financial year, including approximately Rs 1.45 trillion through 235 IPOs.

Pandey questioned whether a market twice its present size could remain fair, stable and trusted while serving a larger economy and financing more enterprises.
items.title: Sebi Considering Dedicated Exchange for Pre-IPO Shares

items.summary:
A research team led by South Korea's Yonsei University has developed a novel optical and thermal simulation framework to optimize perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells for satellite power systems. The group said the framework integrates angle-of-incidence-dependent simulations of external quantum efficiency and short-circuit current density with orbit-specific beta-angle modeling and transient orbital thermal analysis, allowing them to identify an optimal absorber structure for a given metal halide perovskite composition under the air mass zero solar spectrum.

The scientists used COMSOL Multiphysics software to calculate light absorbed by the perovskite top cell and transmitted to the silicon bottom cell. They modeled single-axis tracking with heat inputs from direct radiation, Earth-reflected sunlight, Earth's infrared radiation, and radiative losses, testing a methylammonium lead iodide absorber at 300 K across incidence angles of 0, 20, 40, 60, and 80 degrees and thicknesses ranging from 200 nm to 700 nm. They then compared this with formamidinium lead iodide and two mixed-halide perovskites containing 17% and 24% bromide, whose bandgaps ranged from 1.52 eV to 1.67 eV, evaluating current-matching thicknesses at -100 C, 0 C, and 100 C.

The team applied the framework to three satellites: Starlink-33674 in low Earth orbit, Iridium-181 in near-polar LEO, and Galileo-31 in medium Earth orbit. The results showed that the 1.67 eV perovskite containing 24% bromide achieved the highest simulated average short-circuit current density across all three satellites, reaching 20.22 mA/cm² for Starlink, 15.13 mA/cm² for Iridium, and 16.34 mA/cm² for Galileo.

The researchers concluded that a higher perovskite bandgap increases matched photocurrent, voltage, and radiative-limit projected efficiency under AM0 illumination, while the broader thickness tolerance for current matching comes at the expense of a larger optimal absorber thickness under on-orbit thermal conditions. Their findings were presented in 'Photonic simulation and design framework for optimizing perovskite/Si tandem solar cells for satellite power systems,' published in Communications Engineering.
items.title: Yonsei-led team builds simulation framework for satellite tandem solar cells

items.summary:
Horia Grigorescu of Bucharest law firm Grigorescu Partners argues that a Romanian solar project marketed as 'ready to build' tells investors little about the work still needed to finance and deliver it, because development status does not reveal when electricity can be exported or which costs remain unresolved.

>

The scale of Romania's pipeline is substantial: energy regulator ANRE reported 1,625 projects with valid grid connection approvals in its October update, of which 749 had both connection contracts and building permits. The figures cover renewable and storage projects with approved export capacity of at least 1 MW but do not represent solar plants under construction.

Financing activity is evident: Econergy announced agreements totaling approximately €229 million ($250.6 million) for Părau 2, combining 342 MW of solar with 150 MW of storage. The EBRD secured a contract for difference at €49.40/MWh for 125 MWac while the remaining capacity carries merchant exposure, supported by an InvestEU first-loss guarantee of up to €115 million over its A/B loan structure.

Grigorescu distinguishes grid connection approval (an ATR) from operating under modeled conditions, noting that a plant's equipment may be installed before network reinforcements for full export capacity are completed. He illustrates this with an example 100 MWp project generating 140 GWh at €60/MWh to yield €8.4 million in annual gross revenue, of which €2.1 million could fall outside schedule if export delays prevent delivery of 35 GWh—a sensitivity analysis rather than a market forecast.

He also examines storage: DNV's February assessment modeled a two-hour battery using 2025 prices, yielding annualized revenues of approximately €120,000 ($141,000) to €180,000 per megawatt as historical optimization outcomes rather than realized profits. Grigorescu cautions that the apparent market price spread is not equivalent to a battery's net return once charging costs and degradation are accounted for.

Grigorescu concludes that buyers should establish what 'ready to build' means at closing, assign budgets and deadlines to each outstanding item, and demonstrate a clear path from acquisition to first revenue before using RTB status as a valuation basis. He notes Scatec's EBRD loan of up to €34 million for 189.7 MW alongside loans from the EIB and BCR as another financing example that does not establish equivalent terms elsewhere.
items.title: Romanian solar and storage financing readiness

items.summary:
The espionage drama 'Vivant,' produced by TBS, follows inept businessman Yusuke Nogi (Masato Sakai), who is revealed to be an elite spy for the covert organization Beppan. The series is tasked with protecting Japan from terrorist threats and promoting world peace.

According to the source, the second season of the show has generated several real-world controversies beyond its premise. It reportedly exacerbates already tense relations between Japan and China while also inviting scrutiny over its depictions of LGBTQ+ characters and artificial intelligence.
items.title: Spy Drama 'Vivant' Sparks Real-World Controversy
